surfaces.part: back wall top band (thin grey cap)
ice floor (flat horizontal ground plane, no volume beneath it)

answer.evidence: This is a room-interior tile, not a standing gate, pavilion or building. Rows 12-14 are a thin 3-row grey band, which is a rim on top of the back wall and not a real top surface or roof slope. Rows 15-47 are the brown rock wall seen face-on, and 33 rows of it form the only front face. Rows 48-175 are a large flat ice floor drawn as a top-down plane with no front face beneath it. The thin vertical strips at the left and right edges and the bottom edge are frame lines, not receding side faces. The structure has no roof, lintel or top slope. A kind of 'structure' (gate, pavilion, building) does not fit well.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts put the candidate well below both references. It has 6 colours per tile against 18 and 11, and 57 distinct colours against 185 and 66. All of its dark edge pixels (100%) are neutral, whereas the references sit at 7-9%. The thick near-black frame around the room and the grey-black border read as a sticker-like outline instead of a dark tone of the adjacent material. The ice floor does have dithering, cracks and speckle, so its texture is some but not rich, and it uses roughly 4 light-blue steps against the references' 5-6. The brown rock wall band is a narrow strip with limited tonal steps. Flat-fill coverage is 11% against 0% for both references, mostly from the black frame. Overall the piece is thinner and flatter than the Beodeul references.

surfaces.part: wall top cap (thin light border above the rock wall)
ice floor (horizontal plane seen from above, large)

answer.evidence: Rows 12-14 are a 3-row wall-top cap: a light line at row 12 fading darker through 14 above the wall face. Rows 15-47 are the south face of the back rock wall, 33 rows tall and clearly vertical. Rows 48-175 are a large icy floor plane seen from above, with a dark shadow line at rows 45-47 at the wall base. The side borders are thin 1-px rims with no receding side face. The room has a top plane (floor plus wall cap) and a 33-row front face, so it reads as a 3/4 room. The caveat is that the near (south) wall is absent and the floor is drawn as an open plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is an ice-cave room: a rock band on top, an ice floor, and a thick near-black frame around it. Measured facts back the shallow reading. It has 6 colours per tile against 18 and 11 for the references, 57 distinct colours against 185 and 66, and 100% neutral dark edge pixels against 7% and 9%. That means the outline is a neutral black line, not the tinted dark material tone Beodeul uses. The ice floor has dithered speckle, cracks and a few shading steps (roughly 4), but much of it is a pale blue wash. Flat-fill coverage is 11%, against 0% for the references. The rock band has some clumpy brown variation but only about 3-4 steps. Compared with the references' scalloped tiles, per-tile highlights, and stone shaded one by one, the candidate reads flatter and more sticker-like, with its black border. It is much lower in density, so it fails.

answer.evidence: Rows 0-11 are dark background. Rows 12-14 are a thin gray border strip. Rows 15-47 are a brown rock wall drawn as a vertical face with a dark shadow at rows 45-47. Rows 48 to about 170 are a large, flat ice floor seen from above. It fills most of the 192x176 sprite. The bottom has only a 1-2 row rim and the sides only thin 1-px rims, so there is no south front face of 3 or more rows. There is no roof, lintel, or ceiling slope. The result is a flat floor slab with a back wall strip, not a 3/4 structure with a top and a front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is an ice-room floor with a rock-wall band, not a building with roof, walls and door, so it does not match the reference kind. The measured facts are well below both references: median 6 colours per tile against 18 and 11, and 57 distinct colours against 185 and 66. Flat-fill coverage is 11% against 0% for both references. The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral against 7-9%, which fits the near-black frame and border seen in the picture. The ice floor does have dithered speckle and cracks in about 4 pale-blue steps, so texture is present. The rock band at the top is dark with only a few brown steps, and the large near-black frame areas are flat fills. Beodeul uses 5-6 steps per material with outlines in the dark tone of the adjacent material, and this piece has fewer steps and sticker-like neutral black borders. It would look flatter and shallower next to the references.

answer.evidence: The room is a single cell with a gray wall-top band at rows 12-14 (lighter row 12, darker rows 13-14) above a dark rock wall face at rows 15-47, which is 33 rows tall. Below it is a large ice floor at rows 48-175 seen from above. The side walls are 1-2 px lines with no receding side faces, and the bottom edge is a thin 1-row border with no front face. The wall top band is thin, only 3 rows, but it has an edge line and shadow, and the floor adds a big horizontal surface, so the piece has top surfaces plus a south-facing vertical wall face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts put the candidate well below both references. It has 6 colours per tile against 18 and 11, and 57 distinct colours against 185 and 66. Its dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references. That matches the picture: a uniform near-black frame surrounds the room, and the thin grey-lavender rim lines carry no material tint. The ice floor does have dither speckle, crack lines and a few light-blue steps, so the texture is some rather than flat. But it is a pale blue wash in about 4 steps, not the 5-6 steps of the references. Its 11% flat-fill coverage comes from the black border and the dark wall band, where the references have none. The rock wall band is a thin strip with muddy brown blobs and little per-stone shading, so it reads as a pattern, not as individually shaded stones. The piece is a room floor and wall strip, not a whole building with roof, walls and door, so the kind match is loose, and it falls short of the references on outline, density and shading depth.
